input.learning_objective: What is parameter sharing in CNNs?

chunks: Parameter sharing is a key idea behind convolutional neural networks. Instead of learning a separate weight for every pixel, a single filter is applied across all spatial locations of the input. This drastically reduces the number of parameters compared to a fully connected layer.

Convolution uses the same set of weights (the kernel) at every position in the input. Because the kernel is much smaller than the input image, and the same kernel is reused everywhere, CNNs have far fewer parameters than densely connected networks for image data.
Another consequence of parameter sharing is translation equivariance: if a feature appears in one part of the image, the same filter will detect it in any other location as well.

answer.generated: In convolutional neural networks, parameter sharing means that a single filter's weights are reused across every spatial location of the input, rather than learning separate weights for each input position. In a fully connected layer, every input unit connects to every output unit with its own weight, producing a parameter count proportional to the product of the two layer sizes. By contrast, a convolutional filter has a fixed, small number of weights determined only by the kernel size and channel count, regardless of the spatial size of the input. This weight reuse dramatically lowers the total parameter count and also provides translation equivariance for the detected features.
